title: Conducting Multiple Imaging Modes with One Fluorescence Microscope
protocol: Prepare a vibration-isolated optical table.
Install a microscope body equipped with an illumination arm, a 100X oil-immersion TIRF objective lens, and DIC components.
Place four laser heads (647 nm, 561 nm, 488 nm, and 405 nm) on the optical table.
Ensure the emitted laser beams have the same height and are as short as possible for stability.
If a laser head sits at a shorter height than other lasers, place an aluminum plate underneath it to equalize the height.
Ensure maximum contact between heat sinks and the optical table for optimal heat dissipation.
Install a data acquisition card through a PCI interface.
Connect lasers to the data acquisition card.
Control laser ON/OFF behaviors with TTL output.
Adjust laser power using the analog output of the card.
Mount mirrors and dichroic beam splitters on their respective mounts.
Use stable mirror mounts for mirrors.
Use circular splitters with retaining rings for dichroic beam splitters.
Place mirrors and dichroic beam splitters on the optical table to combine laser beams.
Arrange lasers so that shorter wavelength lasers are closer to the fiber coupling point.
Mount a fiber adapter plate in a z-axis translation mount.
Mount an achromatic doublet lens in a cage plate.
Connect the two parts with extension rods to form a cage.
Mount the cage on the optical table using mounting brackets on the 1-inch thick optical posts.
Align the 647-nm laser with a single-mode optical fiber, connecting FC/APC end to the coupler.
Adjust angles of mirrors and dichroic beam splitters by knobs.
Adjust distance between achromatic doublet lens and fiber adapter plate by z-axis translation mount for maximum laser power output through fiber.
Install a pair of irises temporarily after first laser alignment.
Align remaining lasers one at a time, checking efficiency with a power meter.
Leave one iris in front of the adapter plate to reduce laser reflections.
Connect the other end of the optical fiber to the illumination arm of the microscope.
Design the mag lens, which can fit into the illumination arm using computer-aided design and drafting software.
Place two achromatic lenses in the home-made mag lens holder, one concave with a focal length of -25 mm and one convex with a focal length of 50 mm, maintaining a distance of 25 mm between them.
Install the mag lens to expand the laser beam by a factor of 2.
Remove the mag lens to resume regular illumination without expanding the beams.
Place another filter set in an emission splitter.
Check step 4 for details on the emission splitter modes.
Use a commercial emission splitter in “engaged” mode with a triple cube containing two dichroic beam splitters and three emission filters.
Install an empty slot in the barrier filter wheel when using the triple cube.
Replace the triple cube with a bypass cube for sequential multi-color imaging.
Install the EMCCD camera as the last part of the emission path.
Utilize the USB-PCI connection to achieve fast frame rates.
Adjust excitation lasers’ incidental angle to epi-mode in the illumination arm.
Disengage the 3-D lens if it is engaged (Figure 3C, right panel).
Insert the bypass cube in the emission splitter for diffraction-limited imaging with epi-excitation (Figures 4A and 4E, bottom panel).
(Optional) Insert the mag lens to broaden the illumination area (Figure 2D, left panel).
Move to an “empty” position in the barrier filter wheel.
Adjust the excitation lasers’ incidental angle to the TIRF angle.
Disengage the mag lens and the 3-D lens.
Engage the three-channel mode in the emission splitter.
Replace the bypass cube with a “calibration cube.”
Turn on the camera under DIC.
Adjust the aperture of the emission splitter until three fully separated channels appear on the screen.
Turn the vertical/horizontal adjustment control knobs on the emission splitter and roughly align the three channels.
Place a sample with 100-nm multichannel beads on top of the 100X objective lens and focus on the sample.
Zoom in on one of the bright beads and finely align the three channels by turning the adjustment control knobs again.
Adjust the laser power and exposure time to achieve acceptable signal-to-noise and photobleaching levels.
Use the microscopy imaging software to take time-lapse images.
Insert the 3-D lens and remove the mag lens for SR imaging setup.
Set the exposure time of the camera in the appropriate laser channels (e.g., 5 - 60 ms).
Determine and manually set the optimal excitation lasers’ incidental angle to be the TIRF angle.
Place the sample in SR imaging buffer.
Allow the buffer to equilibrate for at least 10 min before imaging.
Take a DIC image before SR imaging.
Use DIC imaging to find the middle plane of the cells by identifying the height at which cells transition from “light” to “dark” images and appear transparent.
Determine the desired focal plane for SR imaging.
Engage the z-drift correction system once the desired focal plane is determined.
Conduct SR imaging.
Change the 405-nm laser power manually or automatically to maintain a reasonable density of 'blinking-on' spots.
Start the imaging acquisition with 0 W/cm² violet laser power.
Count the number of blinking-on spots in a certain period.
Increase the violet laser power when the number of blinking-on spots drops below the counting threshold.
Terminate the acquisition when the number of blinking-on spots drops below the counting threshold using the maximum violet laser power.
Immobilize multiple 100-nm multichannel beads on the glass coverslip, avoiding forming clusters.
Take images of the beads in different excitation channels.
Extract (X, Y, Z) coordinates by software from bead images.
Plot ΔXi = X1i - X2i and ΔYi = Y1i - Y2i for each bead across color channels separately.
Fit plots with proper functions and save the functions.
Apply the saved functions to correct chromatic aberration in (X, Y) for two-color SR imaging of samples.
Obtain ΔZ = Z1 - Z2 for multichannel beads or reference samples seeded together with the sample of interest to correct z-directional chromatic aberration.
